newsitem.title: CONGO: Signs of hope in bloody Brazzaville showdown.
newsitem.headline: Signs of hope in bloody Brazzaville showdown.

text.p: Mediators pursued an elusive deal to end a bloody month-old standoff in the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville on Friday after another night of shellfire but amid signs that a settlement might be in sight.
"The serious stuff will start as of today," Hellot Mampouya, spokesman for Brazzaville mayor and national mediator Bernard Kolelas told Reuters early on Friday.

Mampouya, speaking after Kolelas held talks with former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso on a nine-point peace blueprint, said he had reason to be optimistic that a resolution to the conflict was getting closer. He did not elaborate.

In New York, the U.N. Security Council agreed in principle on Thursday to endorse a multinational, mainly African, force for the former French colony but question marks remained over who would pay for the force and who would lead it.
President Pascal Lissouba, whose supporters have been locked in a month of bloody clashes with Sassou loyalists, accepted the Kolelas blueprint on Tuesday as a basis for negotiation.
Sassou told national radio on Friday he had replied to Kolelas and his mediation committee in talks on Thursday. He declined to say what but implied he was well disposed to it.

"At the current stage in the negotiations, I have given my answer to the mediation committee," he said, adding: "We are working to lead our people back to peace, to national reconciliation and to well-being."
A month of fighting and indiscriminate shellfire has killed hundreds of people. Tens of thousands have fled their homes.
Gabonese President Omar Bongo, the international mediator, is trying to orchestrate a permanent cease-fire starting on July 5.
Brazzaville was calm on Friday after automatic weapons fire punctuated by bursts of shelling during the night. Residents said it was impossible to tell which faction was responsible.
One striking change on Friday was a new impartial tone on Radio Congo, the state radio, which in recent weeks has broadcast virulent anti-Sassou propaganda throughout the day.

Radio Congo also highlighted an agreement between France and the United States, often portrayed at loggerheads over foreign policy in Central Africa, "to work hand-in-hand" to try to find a peaceable solution to the Congolese conflict.
The showdown began on June 5 when soliders surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militia ahead of a presidential election planned for July 27.
Lissouba, Sassou and Kolelas, whose own supporters were at the heart of similar bloody ethnic and political clashes after a disputed parliamentary election in 1993, were all due to run.
An African peace force in Brazzaville, according to U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, would need voluntary financing and a lead country to organise the operation.
Neither was immediately available, although diplomats said Lissouba's government has offered $1 million for peacekeepers.

"There was a general agreement in the council about the deployment of such a force and there was a willingness among the members...to act rapidly and constructively on the basis of proposals by the secretary-general in this respect," Council President Peter Osvald of Sweden said.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan was expected to report shortly to the council on his proposals.

Sahnoun briefed council members and told a news conference later that the 1,000 soldiers should secure Brazzaville airport to make sure new weapons did not arrive and patrol with opposing factions to verify that a ceasefire was honoured.
